name: Tetrahydrogestrinone (THG / The Clear)

lead: THG is a steroid made by modifying gestrinone so that doping labs would not recognise it. It surfaced in 2003 when a used syringe was handed to anti-doping officials, and it became the centrepiece of the BALCO scandal.
It is mostly known from doping history and detection research rather than from appearance or bodybuilding use.

paras: It binds the androgen receptor about as tightly as DHT, also activates progesterone receptors, and binds the glucocorticoid receptor. Rat studies showed it promotes muscle growth.

It has never been tested in clinical trials, so its effects in people are uncharacterised; infertility, acne and hirsutism are listed with prolonged use. It is a US Schedule III substance and banned in sport.

lead: Tetrahydrogestrinone (THG), nicknamed "The Clear", is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid made by chemically modifying the gynecological drug gestrinone. It was never approved for medical use [1][2].

It became known in 2003 as the first prominent "designer steroid": a compound built so that existing doping tests would not detect it. A spent syringe containing it was passed to the US Anti-Doping Agency, and Don Catlin's UCLA laboratory identified it by mass spectrometry; the findings were published in 2004 [1][3]. The episode was central to the BALCO scandal, which involved sprinters and baseball players [1].

Laboratory studies show THG binds strongly to the androgen receptor and also to progesterone and glucocorticoid receptors, and it promoted muscle growth in rats [1][2]. No human clinical safety or efficacy trials exist.

paras: Wikipedia reports that chemist Patrick Arnold made THG as a designer drug on the reasoning that testers could not find a compound they did not know about, producing it from gestrinone by catalytic hydrogenation; BALCO (Bay Area Laboratory Co-operative), which marketed itself as a supplement company, is said to have distributed it [1][2].

In 2003 sprint coach Trevor Graham gave a used syringe to USADA. Catlin's laboratory identified the contents, synthesised the compound for comparison and developed urine screening using liquid chromatography and tandem mass spectrometry [1][3].

Athletes named in connection with THG include sprinters Marion Jones (who later admitted use before the 2000 Olympics) and Dwain Chambers, and baseball players Barry Bonds and Jason Giambi (who admitted steroid use in 2004) [1]. Arnold was sentenced in August 2006 [1]. Subsequent doping-control research developed methods to screen for unknown "designer" steroids [4][5].

THG binds the androgen receptor with affinity comparable to dihydrotestosterone and is reported to activate androgen and progesterone receptors more potently than nandrolone or trenbolone [1][2]. Unusually for an AAS, it also binds the glucocorticoid receptor strongly, which has been linked in the literature to possible immunosuppressive effects [1][2]. It has no estrogenic activity [1]. Studies in rats found it stimulated muscle growth and increased prostate and seminal vesicle weights [2].

THG (13β,17-diethyl-17β-hydroxygon-4,9,11-trien-3-one) has the formula C21H28O2 and a molar mass of 312.45 g/mol. It is derived from gestrinone by hydrogenating the ethynyl side chain, and resembles trenbolone [1][2][3].

Because it was never clinically tested, its effects in people are not characterised. Wikipedia lists infertility, acne and hirsutism as reported with prolonged use [1]. A Mayo Clinic Proceedings review discusses cardiovascular toxicities of performance-enhancing substances in sport more generally [6].
THG is a Schedule III anabolic steroid in the United States [1]; Grokipedia reports that its emergence prompted regulatory reclassification [2].
No studies found of THG as a treatment or in controlled human use. Research has consisted of analytical detection work, receptor assays and rodent studies [2][3][4][5].

timeline.event: Spent syringe delivered to USADA; THG identified at the UCLA lab [1][3].
Discovery, synthesis and urine detection published [3].
Rat studies report muscle accretion and genomic signature [1].
